The question whether these allegations are sufficient to state a claim 
for promissory estoppel requires a close look at the doctrine's evolution 
in the law of Massachusetts. In Loranger Const. Corp. v. E.F. Hauserman 
Co., 376 Mass. 757 (1978), the Supreme Judicial Court recognized the 
enforceability of a promise on the basis of detrimental 
reliance, but 
declined to "use the expression 'promissory estoppel,' since it tends to 
confusion rather than clarity." Id. at 760-61, 384 N.E.2d 176. The court 
reasoned that "[w]hen a promise is enforceable in whole or in part by 
virtue of reliance, it is a 'contract,' and it is enforceable pursuant to a 
'traditional contract theory' antedating the 
modern 
doctrine of 
consideration." Id. at 761, 384 N.E.2d 176. Since Loranger the court has
